questions.question_text: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols because
questions.question_html: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols because

options.label: A
options.html: Formation of dimers

options.label: B
options.html: Intermolecular hydrogen bonding

options.label: C
options.html: More covalent nature

options.label: D
options.text: More resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base
options.html: More resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base

questions.explanation_text: Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols because their conjugate base is more resonance stabilised. So the correct option is: $\text{Option D: More resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base}$ When a carboxylic acid loses a proton, it forms a carboxylate ion: $\text{RCOOH} \rightarrow \text{RCOO}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$ In the carboxylate ion, the negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms: $\text{R-C}(=O)-O^{-}↔\text{R-C}(-O^{-})=O$ Both resonance structures are equivalent, so the carboxylate ion is highly stable. Phenol also forms a conjugate base, called phenoxide ion: $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$ In phenoxide ion, the negative charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, but the resonance structures are not equivalent. Also, in some resonance forms, the negative charge comes on carbon atoms, which is less stable than having it on oxygen. So, the conjugate base of carboxylic acid is more stable than the conjugate base of phenol. A more stable conjugate base means the acid can lose $\text{H}^{+}$ more easily. Hence, carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols due to more resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base.
questions.explanation_html:
Carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols because their conjugate base is more resonance stabilised.

So the correct option is:

$\text{Option D: More resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base}$

When a carboxylic acid loses a proton, it forms a carboxylate ion:

$\text{RCOOH} \rightarrow \text{RCOO}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$

In the carboxylate ion, the negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms:

$\text{R-C}(=O)-O^{-}↔\text{R-C}(-O^{-})=O$

Both resonance structures are equivalent, so the carboxylate ion is highly stable.

Phenol also forms a conjugate base, called phenoxide ion:

$\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{O}^{-}+\text{H}^{+}$

In phenoxide ion, the negative charge is delocalised into the benzene ring, but the resonance structures are not equivalent. Also, in some resonance forms, the negative charge comes on carbon atoms, which is less stable than having it on oxygen.

So, the conjugate base of carboxylic acid is more stable than the conjugate base of phenol. A more stable conjugate base means the acid can lose $\text{H}^{+}$ more easily.

Hence, carboxylic acids are more acidic than phenols due to more resonance stabilisation of their conjugate base.

questions.question_text: Statement - I : Reduction of ester by DIABL-H followed by hydrolysis gives aldehyde. Statement - II : Oxidation of benzyl alcohol with aqueous $KMnO_{4}$ leads to the formation to Benzaldehyde. Among the above statements, identify the correct statement.
questions.question_html:
Statement - I : Reduction of ester by DIABL-H followed by hydrolysis gives aldehyde.

Statement - II : Oxidation of benzyl alcohol with aqueous $KMnO_{4}$ leads to the formation to Benzaldehyde.

Among the above statements, identify the correct statement.

options.label: A
options.text: Both statements - I and II are false
options.html: Both statements - I and II are false

options.label: B
options.text: Statement - I is true but statement - II is false
options.html: Statement - I is true but statement - II is false

options.label: C
options.text: Statement - I is false but statement - II is true
options.html: Statement - I is false but statement - II is true

options.label: D

options.html: Both statements - I and II are true.

questions.explanation_text: Statement I is true, and Statement II is false. DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) at low temperature selectively reduces an ester to the corresponding aldehyde upon work-up. Aqueous KMnO₄ oxidizes benzyl alcohol all the way to benzoic acid, not benzaldehyde. Answer: Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
Statement I is true, and Statement II is false.

DIBAL-H (diisobutylaluminium hydride) at low temperature selectively reduces an ester to the corresponding aldehyde upon work-up.

Aqueous KMnO₄ oxidizes benzyl alcohol all the way to benzoic acid, not benzaldehyde.

Answer: Option B.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has most acidic Hydrogen ?
questions.question_html: Which of the following has most acidic Hydrogen ?

options.label: A
options.html: Propanoic acid

options.label: B
options.html: Dichloroacetic acid

options.label: C
options.html: Trichloroacetic acid

options.label: D
options.html: Chloroacetic acid

questions.explanation_text: Trichloroacetic acid (Option C) is the strongest acid. Here’s why: Electron-withdrawing effect Chlorine atoms pull electron density away from the –COOH group, stabilizing the conjugate base (the carboxylate anion). More Cl → greater stabilization → stronger acid. Comparative pKa values Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH: pKa ≈ 4.87 Chloroacetic acid, ClCH₂COOH: pKa ≈ 2.86 Dichloroacetic acid, Cl₂CHCOOH: pKa ≈ 1.25 Trichloroacetic acid, CCl₃COOH: pKa ≈ 0.66 Since trichloroacetic acid has the lowest pKa, it donates its proton most readily and is thus the most acidic.
questions.explanation_html:
Trichloroacetic acid (Option C) is the strongest acid. Here’s why:

Electron-withdrawing effect

Chlorine atoms pull electron density away from the –COOH group, stabilizing the conjugate base (the carboxylate anion).

More Cl → greater stabilization → stronger acid.

Comparative pKa values

Propanoic acid, CH₃CH₂COOH: pKa ≈ 4.87

Chloroacetic acid, ClCH₂COOH: pKa ≈ 2.86

Dichloroacetic acid, Cl₂CHCOOH: pKa ≈ 1.25

Trichloroacetic acid, CCl₃COOH: pKa ≈ 0.66

Since trichloroacetic acid has the lowest pKa, it donates its proton most readily and is thus the most acidic.

questions.explanation_text: The lower members of the aliphatic carboxylic acid family, specifically those with carbon chains up to C4, are highly soluble in water. This high solubility is primarily attributed to the formation of hydrogen bonds between the carboxyl group (COOH) of the acid and water molecules.
